title: Associations of physical exercise and sedentary behavior with problematic smartphone use and interaction anxiety in a predominantly first-year convenience sample of Chinese college students: A cross-sectional study
content:
by Qi Han

Problematic smartphone use and interaction anxiety are common concerns in university settings, but their joint relationships with exercise and sedentary behavior remain unclear. We examined these associations in a predominantly first-year convenience sample recruited through 36 universities in four Chinese provinces. The analytical sample included 1,025 students aged 18 years or older, of whom 902 (88.0%) were first-year students. Physical exercise was represented by an adapted self-reported exercise-volume index derived from exercise intensity, duration, and frequency. Sedentary behavior was assessed with a single item whose response categories used inconsistent daily and weekly time frames; it was therefore analyzed as an exploratory categorical indicator. Problematic smartphone use and interaction anxiety were measured with the 22-item Smartphone Addiction Scale for College Students and the conventionally scored 15-item Interaction Anxiousness Scale. Multivariable linear regression models used HC3 heteroscedasticity-robust standard errors and adjusted for sex, academic-year status, and major type. Higher exercise-index values were associated with lower problematic smartphone use (B = −0.120, 95% CI [−0.177, −0.063], p < 0.001) and lower interaction anxiety (B = −0.066, 95% CI [−0.097, −0.035], p < 0.001). When problematic smartphone use was added to the interaction-anxiety model, its association with interaction anxiety was positive (B = 0.305, 95% CI [0.268, 0.342], p < 0.001), while the exercise-index coefficient was attenuated but remained inverse (B = −0.029, 95% CI [−0.055, −0.003], p = 0.027). The overall sedentary-behavior term was not statistically significant in the primary categorical models and varied across sensitivity specifications. Taken together, the results show modest exercise-related associations, no stable sedentary-behavior association, and a positive relationship between problematic smartphone use and interaction anxiety in this sample.
